notes.meaning: Daniel had this vision early in King Belshazzar's reign, before the feast in chapter 5, so the book is not in strict time order here. God gave him clear pictures in a dream. Daniel wrote down the main points so God's people, in his day and later, would have them. One purpose was to warn the Jews that going home from exile would not end all their troubles.

A sea whipped up by winds from every direction pictures the nations of the world stirred up by war and the struggle for power. Out of that storm come four beasts, one after another. They stand for four great empires. They are shown as wild animals because they so often rule by cruelty and force. This is the same series of kingdoms as the statue in chapter 2, but now seen the way God sees them.

The lion with eagle's wings is Babylon, the 'golden head' of chapter 2. It was strong like a lion and quick to conquer like an eagle under Nebuchadnezzar. Tearing off its wings means its fast conquests came to a stop. Standing like a man may recall Nebuchadnezzar being humbled and then given back a human mind in chapter 4. Others take it to mean Babylon lost its lion-like courage and became ordinary.

The bear is the empire of the Medes and Persians, the silver chest and arms of chapter 2. Being raised on one side pictures a two-part empire in which the Persian side became the stronger. The three ribs in its mouth are peoples it had swallowed up, often named as Babylon, Lydia and Egypt. 'Gorge yourself on flesh' means God allowed it to conquer many more lands.

The leopard is the Greek empire of Alexander the Great. Its four wings show how amazingly fast he conquered, even faster than Babylon. The four heads are the four generals who split up his empire after he died. Its power 'was given' by God, since Alexander's small army beat the huge forces of Persia.

The fourth beast is so terrible that Daniel cannot compare it to any animal. The long-held church reading is that it is the Roman Empire. Its iron teeth match the iron legs of the statue in chapter 2. It crushed the nations and trampled what was left. Horns stand for power, and its ten horns are explained in verse 24.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars count Media and Persia as two separate empires. That makes the fourth beast the Greek kingdoms that came after Alexander, not Rome.

notes.meaning: A small horn grows up among the ten and pulls up three of them by the roots. Its human eyes suggest sharp intelligence and cunning. Its mouth boasts proudly against God. All agree it pictures a proud ruler or power from the fourth kingdom who sets himself against God and his people.

differ.view: Most Reformation leaders saw the little horn as the papacy (the rule of the popes). Calvin and the Geneva Bible notes instead saw the Roman Caesars, starting with Julius Caesar.
Early Methodist teaching saw the horn as probably the papacy, or possibly the Turkish empire. It took the three uprooted horns to be lands given to the pope.
Older Baptist commentary applies the horn to papal Rome.
Many evangelicals today believe the horn is a future world ruler, the Antichrist (the final great enemy of Christ). They expect him to rise from a revived Roman Empire before Christ returns.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars take the horn to be the Greek-Syrian king Antiochus Epiphanes, who persecuted the Jews around 167 BC. They believe the book was written in his time.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic writers, following early church teachers like Justin Martyr, expect one personal Antichrist still to come.

notes.meaning: The scene turns to heaven's courtroom. Thrones are set up, and God, called the Ancient of Days because he lives forever, sits as Judge. His snow-white clothing shows his perfect purity. His white hair shows wisdom and honor. His blazing throne on fiery wheels shows that his judgment is fearsome and reaches everywhere.

A river of fire pours out from God against his enemies. Countless angels stand ready to serve him. The court sits and the books are opened, which shows that God judges fairly, with everything on record. Many New Testament pictures of the last judgment, like Revelation 20:11-12, draw on this scene.

Daniel keeps watching because of the horn's boasting. Then the beast is killed and thrown into the fire. God takes proud words against himself seriously. The enemies of his people will surely be brought down in his time.

The first three beasts had already lost their power, but they were allowed to live on for a while. Their peoples carried on even after their empires ended. Each one lasted only as long as God had set. Nothing in history runs beyond the limits God has fixed.

Daniel sees one 'like a son of man', a figure in human form, coming with the clouds. Christians have long understood him as Christ. He is 'like' a man because he had not yet been born as one. The clouds point to his divine glory. He is brought before the Ancient of Days, God the Father. Jesus took 'Son of Man' as his favorite name for himself and pointed to this verse before the high priest (Matthew 26:64).

differ.view: The Son of Man comes up to God in heaven at his ascension, when he goes back to the Father to receive his kingdom.
Early Methodist teaching links this coming to Christ's ascension, when he was crowned King to protect his church.
Some evangelicals place this coming at Christ's second coming, when he returns to set up his kingdom on earth.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the angel later gives the kingdom to 'the saints'. They take the human figure to stand for God's faithful people as a group.

notes.meaning: The Son of Man is given rule, glory and a kingdom over every nation and language. The word 'serve' here is used for the worship given to God, so he is honored as God. Unlike the beast empires, his kingdom will never pass away. Jesus spoke of this when he said, 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me' (Matthew 28:18).

The vision left Daniel deeply shaken. 'Within my body' is literally 'in its sheath', a picture of the body holding the soul like a sheath holds a sword. What troubled him was the suffering God's people would face before the kingdom came.

Daniel asked one of the angels standing near God's throne to explain the vision, and the angel told him plainly. It is good to seek the true meaning of what God shows us. We do that by prayer and careful study, and by learning from faithful teachers of God's Word.

The four beasts are four kings, meaning the kingdoms they lead. They rise 'from the earth': they are earthly powers and will return to dust. Babylon already existed, but the angel speaks of the whole series of kingdoms rising and passing away.

Against all these passing empires stands God's promise. His holy people will receive a kingdom that lasts forever. They do not seize it by force. They receive it through the Son of Man, because Christ and his people share both suffering and glory. 'Forever and ever' puts the strongest possible stress on how long it lasts.

Daniel especially wanted to understand the fourth beast and its horns. He adds details not mentioned before: bronze claws, and a horn that looked bigger than the others. What troubled him most was that this horn would attack God's people.

The horn makes war on God's holy people and seems to win, but only 'until' God steps in. The Ancient of Days comes and rules in their favor. The time arrives for them to receive the kingdom. The saints are God's faithful people, gathered from Israel and from every nation.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe these saints cannot be the church, since the enemy defeats them. They see them as believing Israel during a future time of great trouble.

notes.meaning: The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom, unlike all the others. It will swallow up and trample the whole known world. Rome became the first empire to rule so widely, from east to west.
The ten horns are ten kings who come out of the fourth kingdom. After them comes another king who is different from them. He brings down three of those kings and rises above the rest.

differ.view: Calvin and the Geneva Bible notes take 'ten' to mean 'many'. They see the Roman provinces, each governed by a ruler with king-like power.
Many evangelicals believe the ten are future rulers who will reign at the same time over a revived Roman Empire, just before Christ returns.

notes.meaning: This king will speak against God as if he were God himself. He will wear down God's people slowly through long hardship. He will try to change 'times and laws', which only God has the right to set. Yet the saints are handed over to him only for 'a time, times, and half a time', a limit God has fixed. Satan wants to wear out God's people, but God will always keep a church.

differ.view: Many evangelicals take 'time, times, and half a time' as a literal three and a half years of the Antichrist's rule, matching the 42 months of Revelation 13:5.
Early Methodist commentary counted a day for each year, making 1,260 years of papal power, though it put no weight on the dates.
Calvin did not take 'a time' as a year. He saw an unknown length of time, known only to God and cut short for the sake of his people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars who link the horn to Antiochus Epiphanes note that he banned Jewish feasts and the Sabbath. They see this as what 'change the appointed times and laws' describes.

notes.meaning: Then God's court sits. The king's power is taken away and destroyed forever. Many kingdoms fall and rise again, but this one will never come back. God will set right everything this enemy disordered.

All the power and greatness the world's kingdoms once had will be given to God's holy people. The kingdom is God's, and he shares it with his people through Christ their King. It is everlasting, and every ruler will serve and obey him. It begins as the gospel spreads and reaches its full glory at Christ's return.

differ.view: The promise began to come true when the gospel spread through the world. It will be complete at the end, and it is a spiritual kingdom, not earthly power for believers.
Some evangelicals believe it will be fulfilled when Christ returns and reigns on earth for a thousand years, followed by the new heavens and earth.

notes.meaning: The vision ends there. Daniel was so shaken that his face went pale. He kept the matter in his heart, as Mary later treasured what was said about Jesus. He was not hiding it but keeping it safe for God's people. He was content with what God chose to show, and the Holy Spirit meant even more by it than Daniel understood.

problems: v. 24: dropped differ point (Methodist): no checkable source
